extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing fiction writers (especially fantasy/sci‑fi novelists and creative writing students)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical set of creative‑writing rules and heuristics for plotting, character, viewpoint, worldbuilding (especially magic systems), prose craft, and professional practice — derived from Brandon Sanderson's BYU lecture notes. Focused on producing satisfying, publishable genre fiction, particularly speculative novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise–Progress–Payoff framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories make three types of promises: tone, character arc, and plot type; the narrative must show progress toward those promises and provide a payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set clear promises early (tone, arc, plot type). Show steady movement (progress) toward an inevitable, exciting goal. Deliver a payoff that satisfies the promises — the payoff can expand beyond the initial promise or use substitution twists to remain surprising yet earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress: maintain forward momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress requires showing steady movement toward an inevitable, exciting goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each scene or sequence advances toward the goal; avoid stasis. Use escalating complications so that solutions generate new problems (see 'Yes, but / No, and' technique).

rubrics_metrics.name: Payoff: satisfy or creatively expand promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Payoff should answer or appropriately transform the story's established promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may expand the scope of what you promised or substitute a different but emotionally equivalent payoff, but the reader must feel the outcome was earned by the setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot archetypes vs. structures — use both appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Archetypes (heist, romance, information plot, etc.) target emotional experiences; structures (Hero's Journey, Three‑Act, etc.) organize narrative mechanics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strip archetypes to their core elements and apply them across genres. Choose a structure to organize pacing and beats; combine archetype and structure deliberately to achieve the intended emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward outlining (ending-first plotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the desired ending, then create bullet points for necessary steps to reach it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize bullets by character, setting, and plot; when writing, rearrange into chronological order. Treat nested plots as separate stories (each with its own promises) and outline them similarly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery writing: 'Yes, but / No, and' escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: When discovery‑writing, use a pattern where characters try solutions that either succeed with new complications ('Yes, but') or fail and escalate the stakes ('No, and').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method creates forward momentum and rising stakes without a complete blueprint; it yields emergent plot while preserving tension and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide which characters need arcs (not everyone must change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all characters require arcs; some iconic figures succeed as largely static (e.g., James Bond, Sherlock).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For those who do need arcs, show desires and obstacles. You can also use a reverse approach (show what characters should want) to reveal internal conflict. Be deliberate about which characters grow and which remain constants for tone/genre reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Viewpoint selection and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate viewpoint form — first person (epistolary/flashback/cinematic), omniscient (present narrator/true omniscient/limited omniscient), or limited third (one character per scene, can shift between scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit perspective within scenes for clarity; pick the viewpoint type that best serves tone and reader access to information. Be consistent within scenes and deliberate about when to shift viewpoint between scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshopping etiquette and feedback use
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshoppers should provide descriptive feedback rather than prescriptive fixes; authors (workshopees) should listen without defending and give feedback time before implementing changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate critique stages (description, questions, suggestions). Authors should consider feedback but not react defensively; allow time to digest before making revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeroeth Law of worldbuilding: prioritize awesome concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the coolest concept and build rules around it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the core interesting idea drive the world and mechanics instead of forcing concepts into a preexisting framework; design systems to showcase that central awesomeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Law of magic systems: reader understanding enables satisfying solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Your ability to solve problems with magic in a satisfying way is directly proportional to how well the reader understands said magic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If magic (or any system) is used as a problem‑solving tool, make its rules and limitations understandable enough that the reader can appreciate clever solutions; the more the reader knows, the more rewarding the resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Law: prefer flaws/limitations/costs to raw power
rubrics_metrics.description: "Flaws or limitations are more interesting than powers." Distinguish flaws (fixable), limitations (permanent), and costs (consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems with constraints and costs to create tension and narrative utility. Use limitations and costs to force tradeoffs and meaningful choices rather than granting unchecked ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third Law: deepen existing elements before adding new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand existing elements before adding new concepts; deep exploration of fewer concepts beats superficial treatment of many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer elaboration and complication of what you've already introduced rather than continually introducing new mechanics or lore that dilute focus and complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hard, soft, or hybrid magic appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard magic: defined rules and predictable costs for problem‑solving. Soft magic: mysterious, wonder‑focused, unpredictable. Hybrids create contrast and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hard systems where puzzle‑like resolutions are central; use soft systems to preserve awe or thematic mystery. Combining both can give room for clever solutions and preserved wonder in appropriate moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid info dumps; reveal worldbuilding through action and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Convey worldbuilding through character perspective and action; avoid encyclopedia‑style exposition or 'maid and butler' dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the 'pyramid of abstraction': start with concrete sensory detail, then move to broader or abstract information. Integrate explanation into scenes and character experience, not isolated exposition blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover core worldbuilding categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilding should address physical aspects (geography, climate, fauna, flora, magic system, cosmology) and cultural aspects (religion, government, economics, social hierarchy, fashion, language, taboos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be sure to think through both physical and cultural dimensions; choose which details to show based on relevance to plot/character and avoid overloading readers with irrelevant minutiae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmit worldbuilding through character lens and concrete language
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'grand skill' of speculative fiction is transmitting worldbuilding engagingly; show through character lens and use concrete language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair character revelation with world detail so each detail also advances character or plot. Ground abstract concepts in sensory, specific images before explaining their larger meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and productivity expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consistent practice compounds skill development; average writing output benchmarks given (300–700 words/hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set modest but consistent weekly commitments to reach large goals (e.g., 100,000‑word novel achievable with steady weekly output). Track and protect writing time; expect variable rates but plan around realistic hourly outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect writing time and set boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure life to protect writing time: mentally demanding jobs reduce writing capacity; menial labor may allow planning headspace. Set boundaries and involve family as guardians of writing time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be intentional about scheduling and communicating needs to family or partners. Create conditions (jobs, routines) that allow consistent creative focus rather than relying on sporadic bursts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence as a professional practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistence matters; non‑publication is not failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain long‑term commitment to craft. Treat rejections and slow progress as part of the writing career rather than terminal judgments; continue producing and improving.
